relevance_reason: Reports three unrelated consanguineous Turkish children with homozygous TYK2 P216Rfs*14 deficiency who had COVID-19 pneumonia and other viral infections, plus fibroblast functional data. This extends the IMD35 phenotype; most of the paper is about other type I IFN genes.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2022) described 3 unrelated children with AR TYK2 deficiency, each born to a different set of consanguineous Turkish parents, among 112 children hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. P2, a 2-year-old girl, had moderate COVID-19 pneumonia that did not need oxygen. She had earlier had neonatal sepsis, 2 ICU admissions for fever and dyspnea before 5 months of age, Kawasaki disease at 11 months, and a hospitalization for infection with the VZV vaccine at age 2. P3 (age 4) and P4 (age 9), both boys, had critical COVID-19 pneumonia needing ICU admission and high-flow oxygen. P3 had earlier had neonatal sepsis and influenza pneumonia needing ICU care at age 3. P4 had recurrent bronchitis needing hospital admission. All 3 survived.
quotes: P2 (female), P3 (male), and P4 (male) were unrelated 2-, 4-, and 9-yr-old children, each born to a different set of consanguineous Turkish parents. All three are homozygous for the same TYK2 LOF mutation.

P2 was hospitalized for moderate COVID-19 pneumonia but did not require oxygen therapy. P3 and P4 were both admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for critical COVID-19 pneumonia requiring high-flow oxygen therapy.

P3 | TYK2 | AR | P216fs/P216fs (LOF) | M | 4 | Middle East/Turkey | Critical | | Admitted to ICU for influenza pneumonia at 3 yr; no adverse reaction to MMR vaccination | Hospitalized for sepsis during the neonatal period | Survived | This report

findings.statement: In 3 unrelated consanguineous Turkish children with COVID-19 pneumonia (P2-P4), Zhang et al. (2022) used whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing to find the same homozygous TYK2 frameshift variant, P216Rfs*14, and confirmed it by Sanger sequencing. Family segregation analysis confirmed AR inheritance. The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression in patient cells, and the authors confirmed that it was loss-of-function. Eight of the 12 patients in the series, including those with other gene defects, were tested for autoantibodies against type I IFNs, and all were negative.
quotes: three unrelated patients had the same homozygous missense variant of TYK2 (P216fs*14; AR inheritance was confirmed for all three patients by family segregation analysis)

Three of the five patients not previously reported, P2, P3, and P4, carried the same TYK2 variant (P216Rfs*14), which had already been shown experimentally to be loss-of-expression in cells from patients (Fuchs et al., 2016). We confirmed that this variant was LOF (not depicted).

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2022) found that the 3-year-old younger sister of P3 had the same homozygous TYK2 genotype. She had a history of critical influenza pneumonia needing intubation and ventilation, as well as disseminated varicella, but she had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and remained seronegative. The authors noted that TYK2 deficiency impairs, but does not abolish, cellular responses to type I IFN. They said more TYK2-deficient patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 were needed to estimate penetrance, and suggested penetrance may be incomplete.
quotes: The third was the 3-yr-old younger sister of P3, who carries the same genotype. She had a history of critical influenza pneumonia that required intubation and ventilation, as well as disseminated varicella.

The occurrence of critical pneumonia in three unrelated patients with TYK2 deficiency is more surprising. Indeed, TYK2 deficiency impairs, but does not abolish, cellular responses to type I IFNs (Boisson-Dupuis et al., 2018).
with complete (e.g., probably IFNAR1 and STAT2 deficiencies) or incomplete (e.g., TLR7 and perhaps TYK2 deficiencies) penetrance, depending on the locus

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2022) studied ACE2-transduced SV40 fibroblasts from a TYK2-deficient patient homozygous for P216fs*14. Like STAT2-deficient cells, they did not control SARS-CoV-2 replication normally. Pretreatment with IFN-alpha-2b did not block the infection, and the cells failed to induce ISGs (IFIT1, MX1, IFI27) after viral infection or IFN-alpha-2b pretreatment. The authors suggested this supported a causal role of TYK2 deficiency in COVID-19 pneumonia.
quotes: We infected SV40 fibroblasts from a TYK2-deficient patient with the same genotype as P2–P4 (homozygous for P216fs*14) with SARS-CoV-2.
We found that cells from STAT2- and TYK2-deficient patients failed to induce ISG production in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection or IFN-α2b pretreatment (Fig. 4 B).
Thus, cells from STAT2- and TYK2-deficient patients were unable to control SARS-CoV-2 infection in a type I IFN-dependent manner in vitro.

findings.statement: Zhang et al. (2022) studied an international cohort of 112 children under 16 years old hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. Twelve (10.7%) had recessive complete inborn errors of type I IFN immunity: XLR TLR7 deficiency (7 children) and AR deficiency of IFNAR1 (1), STAT2 (1), or TYK2 (3). None of these 15 recessive deficiencies was found in 1,224 SARS-CoV-2-infected controls without pneumonia (P = 1.2 x 10(-11)). The authors identified AR TYK2 deficiency as a new genetic cause of COVID-19 pneumonia.
quotes: 4 of the 15 known clinically recessive and biochemically complete inborn errors of type I IFN immunity: X-linked recessive TLR7 deficiency (7 children) and autosomal recessive IFNAR1 (1), STAT2 (1), or TYK2 (3) deficiencies.
Our findings implicate AR STAT2 and TYK2 deficiencies as new genetic etiologies of COVID-19 pneumonia.

relevance_reason: Reports five new TYK2-deficient patients with novel TYK2 mutations and functional characterization of cytokine responses, directly relevant to IMD35.

findings.statement: Lv et al. (2022) described 5 patients with TYK2 deficiency who presented with or without elevated IgE levels and atopy and had distinct pathogen infection profiles, supporting the observation that TYK2-deficient patients do not necessarily show features of hyper-IgE syndrome. Lymphocyte homeostasis was disrupted, with altered T- and B-cell differentiation assessed by flow cytometry.
quotes: We described five more TYK2-deficient cases presenting with or without hyper-IgE levels, atopy, and distinct pathogen infection profile, which are caused by novel TYK2 mutations.
The homeostasis of lymphocytes is also disrupted.

phenotypes.text: elevated IgE levels in some patients

findings.statement: In 5 patients with TYK2 deficiency, Lv et al. (2022) identified novel TYK2 mutations by high-throughput sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Pathogenicity was supported by qRT-PCR, Western blot, and protein stability assays, and patient PBMCs showed heterogeneous responses to IFN-alpha/beta/gamma, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-23.
quotes: These mutations were all found by high-throughput sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
Pathogenic effects of patients were confirmed by qRT-PCR, Western blot, and protein stability assays.
The patients showed heterogeneous responses to various cytokine treatments, including IFN-α/β/γ, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-23.

findings.statement: Lv et al. (2022) proposed that TYK2 acts as a multi-tasker orchestrating various cytokine signaling pathways, with differentially combined defects accounting for the varied clinical manifestations of TYK2 deficiency.
quotes: we propose that TYK2 works as a multi-tasker in orchestrating various cytokine signaling pathways, differentially combined defects which account for the expressed clinical manifestations.

relevance_reason: Reports a new patient with TYK2 deficiency who carries a novel homozygous TYK2 missense variant, with functional expression studies and a review of the clinical features of earlier reported cases.

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) reported a Chinese boy, the second child of young nonconsanguineous parents, who was vaccinated with BCG on day 3 of life. He had repeated abscess and ulceration at the injection site, which healed by 10 months. At 14 months he developed BCG-associated left axillary lymph node tuberculosis, with acid-fast bacilli and Mycobacterium bovis BCG isolated. From age 6 months he had recurrent respiratory tract infections every 1 to 2 months and diarrhea. Pathogens identified included Salmonella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and influenza A and B (IgM positive). He did not have high serum IgE, atopy, staphylococcal disease, lymphopenia, or significant fungal infection. He also had a small head circumference and delayed speech.
quotes: The diagnosis of BCG associated lymph node tuberculosis was made with positive staining for acid-fast bacilli and isolated Mycobacterium Bovis BCG from the discharging axillary sinuses.

He also suffered from recurrent respiratory tract infections (had pneumonia or upper respiratory tract infection every 1–2 months) and diarrhea since the age of 6 months (sensitive to the food firstly contacted).

No high serum IgE concentration, atopy, staphylococcal illness, or lymphopenia was found for him. He started to say some simple words at the age of 3 years and 4 months with normal motor development. Physical examination revealed a small head circumference.

phenotypes.text: BCG disease with injection-site abscess and ulceration
BCG lymphadenitis of axillary lymph node

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) found that at age 1 year 11 months the patient had normal serum IgG, IgA, IgM, and IgE (27.4 IU/ml) and normal eosinophil counts. CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ T-cell percentages were normal, the CD19+ B-cell percentage was increased (26.6%), and the NK-cell percentage was decreased (3.6%).
quotes: Immunoglobin: serum IgG, IgA, IgE, and IgM levels were normal.

the percentage of CD3+T cells, CD3+CD4+CD8−T cells, CD3+CD8+CD4−T cells were within the range of normal, whereas the percentage of CD45−CD19 + cells were higher than the normal range, and CD3−CD16 /CD56+ cells were lower (Table 1).

phenotypes.hpo_label: Reduced total natural killer cell count

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous missense variant in exon 17 of the TYK2 gene, c.2395G>A (p.G799R), in a Chinese boy with BCG disease and recurrent respiratory infections. Both parents were heterozygous for the variant. The authors noted that the variant is listed in gnomAD and therefore is not a private mutation; its CADD score was 25.6. The patient also carried heterozygous variants in CFH, LRRC8A, and NIPBL, for which the authors considered the evidence of pathogenicity insufficient.
quotes: Mutations were found in four genes, including TYK2 (c.2395G>A, p.G799R, hom), CFH (c.2089C>T, p.L697F, het), LRRC8A (c.1250G>A, p.R417Q, het) and NIPBL (c.5575-27_c.5575-26delCT, –, het).
Sequence analysis demonstrated the homozygous missense mutation in the exon 17 of the TYK2 gene of the patient, which was heterozygous in his parents (Figure 1).
As a supplement, this mutation type was is included in the genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), suggesting that this was not a private mutation.

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) found that patient-derived cells had reduced TYK2 mRNA on qRT-PCR, and western blot detected no TYK2 protein. When the c.2395G>A (p.G799R) mutant was expressed in HEK293T cells as FLAG-tagged and GFP-tagged constructs, it lowered both TYK2 mRNA and protein levels compared with wildtype.
quotes: The results showed that this mutation leads to a decrease of TYK2 mRNA expression (Figure 2A). Besides, the western blot results showed that no TYK2 protein expression found in the patient (Figure 2B).

The qRT-PCR results showed that this c.2395G>A mutant decreased the expression of FLAG-TYK2 and TYK2-GFP (Figure 3B). To go along with this, this mutant also decreased the expressed protein of FLAG-TYK2 and TYK2-GFP in the western blot analysis (Figure 3C).

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) reviewed 12 reported patients with TYK2 deficiency, including their own patient; the mean age at diagnosis was 10.8 years. Seven patients (58%) had intracellular bacterial infections, 2 had M. tuberculosis, and 7 (58%) had recurrent viral infections. Two had rash or atopic dermatitis, 3 had markedly increased serum IgE, and 2 had EBV-related B-cell lymphoma with T-cell lymphopenia. None had the facial, skeletal, dental, or vascular features of STAT3-associated hyper-IgE syndrome.
quotes: Including our patient, there are 12 patients reported with TYK2 deficiency (Table 3), with the average age at diagnosis of 10.8 years old. Seven patients (58%) suffered from intracellular bacterial infections. M. tuberculosis was observed in 2 cases (17%). Seven patients had recurrent virus infections (58%).
none of the 12 patients had special facial features, abnormal bone development or pathological fractures, delayed deciduous tooth loss, or aneurysms.

findings.statement: Wu et al. (2020) summarized the main features of TYK2 deficiency as autosomal recessive TYK2 mutation, normal lymphocyte counts with defects in multiple cytokine signaling pathways, susceptibility to viruses or intracellular bacteria, and IgE that may or may not be elevated. They suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in patients with repeated intracellular bacterial (including tuberculosis) or viral infections, or with eczema.
quotes: we summary the main features of TYK2 deficiency: (a) TYK2 gene mutation; (b) Autosomal recessive inheritance; (c) The number of lymphocytes is normal, and multiple cytokine signaling defect; (d) Susceptibility to viruses or intracellular bacteria; (e) With/without elevated IgE.

relevance_reason: The paper describes a patient with TYK2 deficiency, the disorder this entry covers, along with functional studies of cytokine signaling and NK-cell function.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2016) reported a patient with TYK2 deficiency who had eczema, skin abscesses, respiratory infections, and serum IgE levels above 1000 U/mL. The patient had no viral or mycobacterial infections. The authors described the human phenotype as surprisingly mild.
quotes: We investigated a TYK2 deficient patient, presenting with eczema, skin abscesses, respiratory infections and IgE levels >1000 U/mL, without viral or mycobacterial infections

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2016) developed a simple diagnostic monocyte assay and used it to show that the patient's TYK2 mutation completely abolished the IFN-alpha-mediated antiviral response. The mutation also partly reduced IL-10-mediated signaling, which was associated with reduced IL-10R-beta expression. IL-6-mediated signaling was not affected.
quotes: We established a novel simple diagnostic monocyte assay to show that the mutation completely abolishes the IFN-α mediated antiviral response.
It also partly reduces IL-10 but not IL-6 mediated signaling associated with reduced IL-10Rβ expression.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2016) established a simple diagnostic monocyte assay that detects the loss of the IFN-alpha-mediated antiviral response in TYK2 deficiency.
quotes: We established a novel simple diagnostic monocyte assay to show that the mutation completely abolishes the IFN-α mediated antiviral response.

findings.statement: In a TYK2-deficient human cell line, Fuchs et al. (2016) found nearly normal type III IFN signaling and only minimal impairment of virus control. In the patient, NK-cell phenotype and function were normal, including IL-12/IL-18-mediated responses, which contrasts with TYK2-deficient mice. The authors suggested that preserved type III IFN responses and normal NK-cell function may help protect against viruses in TYK2 deficiency and may account for the mild human phenotype.
quotes: we found almost normal type-III IFN signaling associated with minimal impairment of virus control in a TYK2 deficient human cell line
Contrary to observations in TYK2 deficient mice, NK-cell phenotype and function, including IL-12/IL-18 mediated responses, were normal in the patient.
preserved type-III IFN responses and normal NK-cell function may contribute to antiviral protection in TYK2 deficiency leading to a surprisingly mild human phenotype

relevance_reason: Reports seven new patients from five families with autosomal recessive complete TYK2 deficiency, five novel null TYK2 mutations, and detailed functional characterization, defining the core phenotype (mycobacterial and viral infections without HIES).

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that the core clinical phenotype of autosomal recessive complete TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta, and that impaired IL-6 responses and hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans.
quotes: The core clinical phenotype of TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections, caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-α/β. Moreover, impaired IL-6 responses and HIES do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) reported 7 TYK2-deficient patients (P2-P8) from 5 unrelated families from Turkey, Morocco, Iran, and Argentina who had mycobacterial and/or viral infections but none of the features of HIES: none had atopy, high serum IgE, staphylococcal disease, documented pyogenic infections, or fungal infections including mucocutaneous candidiasis. This contrasted with the previously reported Japanese patient (P1), who had atopic dermatitis, high IgE, and staphylococcal abscesses.
quotes: Surprisingly, unlike P1, none of these seven newly identified TYK2-deficient patients displayed any of the features of HIES. In particular, they did not display atopy, high serum IgE concentration, or staphylococcal disease.

None of these newly identified patients (P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, and P8) suffered from documented pyogenic infections, including staphylococcal diseases in particular, or from fungal infections, including mucocutaneous candidiasis in particular.
Serum IgE levels have been determined on multiple occasions and have never been found to be high.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) described a Turkish man (P2), born to first-cousin parents, who had disseminated BCG lymphadenitis at 21 months, Brucella meningitis at 8 years, and shingles of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve at 11 years; he was 23 years old at report.
quotes: The second patient is a Turkish man (P2) born to consanguineous parents (first-degree cousins).

this patient displayed disseminated BCG lymphadenitis at 21 mo of age and severe bacterial meningitis (with CFS cultures positive for Brucella spp.) at 8 yr of age, and at the age of 11 yr, he was diagnosed with shingles affecting the right maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) described Moroccan sibs born to first-cousin parents: a girl (P3) who developed disseminated extrapulmonary M. tuberculosis infection (abdominal disease, ascites, psoas abscess) at 13 years and died after bacterial meningitis 15 months after onset, and her brother (P4) who had meningitis of unknown etiology at 8 months, recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections, asthma, ear canal eczema, and high eosinophils.
quotes: P3 was hospitalized at the age of 13 yr with suspected abdominal tuberculosis.

M. tuberculosis was isolated from the abscess fluid culture, confirming the diagnosis of disseminated extrapulmonary tuberculosis. Treatment was restarted, but the patient was readmitted to hospital with bacterial meningitis and subsequently died, 15 mo after the initial onset of symptoms.

P3’s younger brother (P4) was hospitalized at the age of 8 mo for meningitis of unknown etiology. He suffered from recurrent otitis and urinary tract infections and presented asthma and eczema of the ear canal. His eosinophil levels were found to be high.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) described Iranian sibs born to consanguineous parents: a boy (P5) who developed BCG axillary and cervical lymphadenitis at 2 and 4 months and paravertebral and psoas abscesses with pulmonary involvement at 4.5 years, treated with antimycobacterials, surgery and IFN-gamma; and his sister (P6) who had BCG lymphadenopathy after vaccination and an unknown viral skin infection at 1 year.
quotes: The fifth patient, P5, is a 5-yr-old boy born to consanguineous Iranian parents.
At 2 and 4 mo of age, he developed right axillary lymphadenitis and multiple cervical lymphadenitis, respectively.
At the age of 4.5 yr, he developed paravertebral and psoas abscesses with fistulization and pulmonary involvement.
She developed BCG lymphadenopathy, lasting for 1 mo, after vaccination. At the age of 1 yr, she was hospitalized for 1 wk for an unknown viral infection of the skin.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) described a 9-year-old Iranian girl (P7) born to consanguineous parents who developed miliary tuberculosis, with diffuse bilateral micronodular lung infiltrations, hilar and mediastinal adenopathy, and cavitary consolidation; M. tuberculosis was identified on gastric washes.
quotes: The seventh patient is a 9-yr-old girl from Iran born to consanguineous parents.

At the age of 9 yr, spiral lung CT with contrast showed diffuse bilateral micronodular infiltrations associated with hilar and mediastinal adenopathies and cavitary consolidation in the right upper lobe.
M. tuberculosis was identified on gastric washes by PCR and culture.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) described an 11-year-old Argentinian boy (P8), adopted at 1 day, who had recurrent HSV disease including herpes gingivostomatitis, aseptic herpes meningitis, and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions from 18 months, with good response to acyclovir; he also had mild mental disability of uncertain origin and no mycobacterial disease despite BCG vaccination.
quotes: He successively suffered from herpes gingivostomatitis at 18 mo of age, aseptic meningitis (fever, vomiting, irritability, and altered mental state/reduced consciousness), and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions at 24 mo of age.

at the age of 10 yr, he was admitted with aseptic herpes meningitis and disseminated cutaneous herpetic lesions (HSV PCR: positive). He also has mild mental disability, and it has not been clearly established whether this disability is congenital or occurred after meningitis.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) updated the clinical history of the original Japanese TYK2-deficient patient (P1), born to consanguineous parents, who had atopic dermatitis from 1 month, BCGitis, S. aureus skin abscesses, Salmonella sepsis, PIV3 pneumonia, recurrent oral HSV, molluscum contagiosum, mild oral candidiasis, hypereosinophilia and high serum IgE (1,430-2,100 IU/ml); at 30 years he had ocular sarcoidosis.
quotes: P1 has displayed atopic dermatitis since the age of 1 mo and recurrent bacterial and viral infections since the age of 1 yr.
Immunological explorations have repeatedly revealed hypereosinophilia (701–800/µl) and high serum IgE concentrations (1,430–2,100 IU/ml).
P1 is now 30 yr old and is regularly followed clinically in Japan. He is currently suffering from ocular sarcoidosis.

findings.statement: In a Turkish patient (P2) with BCG disease, Brucella meningitis, and VZV infection, Kreins et al. (2015) identified, by linkage analysis and Sanger sequencing, a homozygous 9-bp deletion in exon 16 of TYK2 (c.2303_2311del), resulting in a premature stop codon at position 767 (L767X). The mutation was absent from public databases, and no TYK2 protein was detectable in the patient's cells.
quotes: There is a 9-bp deletion in exon 16, c.2303_2311del, in P2 from kindred B
The 9-bp deletion of P2 results in a premature stop codon at position 767 of the 1,187–amino acid TYK2 protein

variants.consequence: in-frame deletion creating premature stop codon

findings.statement: In Moroccan sibs (P3 and P4), Kreins et al. (2015) identified by whole-exome sequencing a homozygous 1-bp insertion in exon 23 of TYK2 (c.3318_3319insC), causing a frameshift and a premature stop codon at position 1110 (T1106HfsX4).
quotes: In P3 and P4, from kindred C, there is a frameshift insertion of 1 bp in exon 23, c.3318_3319insC
In P3 and P4, the frameshift generates a premature stop codon at amino acid position 1110.

findings.statement: In Iranian sibs (P5 and P6) with BCG disease, Kreins et al. (2015) identified by whole-exome sequencing a homozygous c.462G>T substitution in exon 5 of TYK2, resulting in a premature stop codon (E154X).
quotes: A nucleotide substitution in exon 5 (c.462G>T) in P5 and P6, from kindred D, leads to the creation of a premature stop codon at amino acid position 154 (E154X).

findings.statement: In an Iranian girl (P7) with miliary tuberculosis, Kreins et al. (2015) identified by whole-exome sequencing a homozygous 1-bp deletion in exon 3 of TYK2 (c.149delC), causing a frameshift and premature stop codon at position 50 (S50HfsX1).
quotes: A frameshift deletion of 1 bp at position 149 in exon 3 in P7 (c.149delC), from kindred E, leads to the creation of a premature stop codon at position 50 in the protein (S50HfsX1).

findings.statement: In an Argentinian boy (P8) with recurrent HSV disease, Kreins et al. (2015) identified by targeted next-generation sequencing a homozygous c.1912C>T substitution in exon 13 of TYK2, creating a premature stop codon (R638X).
quotes: A nucleotide substitution (c.1912 C>T) at position 1912 in exon 13 in P8, from kindred F, creates a premature stop codon at position 638 (R638X; Fig. 1, A–C).

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) found that in all kindreds clinical disease was observed in all homozygotes and only in homozygotes, and concluded that the patients had autosomal recessive TYK2 deficiency; most families were consanguineous.
quotes: In all kindreds, clinical disease was observed in all of the homozygotes, and only in homozygotes.
Thus, the seven patients from five kindreds reported here probably had autosomal recessive (AR) TYK2 deficiency

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) noted that the 5 novel TYK2 mutations were private, absent from their in-house exome database and public databases including 1000 Genomes and ExAC, and that no homozygotes and only 84 heterozygotes for TYK2 stop mutations were present in any database.
quotes: They are also private, as they are absent from our in-house WES database and all public databases (including NCBI, Ensembl, 1,000 genomes, and ExAc). There are no homozygous individuals for stop mutations in any database and only 84 heterozygous individuals.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) showed by Western blotting with 4 antibodies against N- or C-terminal epitopes that the 130-kD TYK2 protein was undetectable in EBV-B cells, HVS-T cells, and fibroblasts of all patients, indicating complete TYK2 deficiency; no abnormal splicing was detected. TYK2-deficient cells had reduced surface IFN-alpha-R1, IL-10R2, and IL-12R-beta-1, rescued by wildtype TYK2, reflecting loss of the TYK2 scaffolding role.
quotes: The 130-kD TYK2 protein, which was detectable in control cells, was undetectable in cells from all patients
These results suggest that the seven newly identified patients (P2–P8), like P1, display complete TYK2 deficiency, with no residual production of the WT protein.
We also found that the ectopic expression of WT TYK2 in these cells rescued the surface expression of IFN-αR1, IL-10R2, and IL-12Rβ1

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) found that TYK2-deficient T and NK cells had impaired but not abolished IFN-gamma production in response to IL-12, in contrast to IL-12R-beta-1 deficiency, which they suggested accounts for mycobacterial disease and its relatively favorable response to antibiotics; the patient with virulent M. tuberculosis (P3) died.
quotes: Thus, complete TYK2 deficiency resulted in impaired but not abolished responses to IL-12 in both T cells and NK cells in these patients. These data might explain both the occurrence of mycobacterial diseases in TYK2-deficient patients and the relatively favorable response of these diseases to antibiotic treatment.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) showed impaired but not abolished IL-23 responses in TYK2-deficient cells, with profoundly impaired IL-17A/F production by naive CD4 T cells in vitro but normal proportions of circulating IL-17+ T cells ex vivo, probably accounting for the lack of overt chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
quotes: Thus, the response to IL-23 is impaired but not abolished in TYK2-deficient patients. This results in an impairment of the generation of IL-17 T cells in vitro but not in vivo, probably accounting for the lack of overt CMC in the patients

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) found reduced but not absent STAT1 phosphorylation and GAF/ISGF3 DNA binding in response to IFN-alpha/beta in patient cells, absent STAT3 phosphorylation, low basal ISG expression, and failure of IFN-alpha to control VSV replication in EBV-B and HVS-T cells, all rescued by wildtype TYK2; they suggested residual responses explain the mild viral phenotype resembling partial STAT1 deficiency. Responses to IFN-lambda were normal although basal IFIT1 levels were low.
quotes: After stimulation with IFN-α and IFN-β, we observed STAT1 phosphorylation in the cells of all patients, albeit at much lower levels than in a healthy control

In contrast to the results obtained for control cells, the prior treatment of EBV–B cells and HVS–T cells from the patients with IFN-α did not lead to control of viral replication after 48 h of infection
Overall, the viral infections seen in four of the eight TYK2-deficient patients can be accounted for by impaired responses to IFN-α/β and, perhaps, IFN-λ.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) showed impaired but not abolished IL-10 responses (STAT3 phosphorylation, SOCS3 induction, TNF suppression in macrophages) in all TYK2-deficient patients, rescued by wildtype TYK2, and suggested residual IL-10 signaling accounts for absence of early-onset colitis. Responses to IL-21, IL-27, IFN-gamma, and LIF were normal.
quotes: The EBV–B cells of all TYK2-deficient patients also had low levels of STAT3 phosphorylation after IL-10 stimulation
Residual cellular responses to IL-10 probably account for the lack of early-onset colitis in TYK2-deficient patients.
In contrast, TYK2 is apparently redundant for signal transduction downstream from receptors stimulated by IFN-γ, IL-27, IL-21, and LIF.

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) found that cells from the 7 new patients responded normally to IL-6, unlike those of P1 who had HIES. Re-expression of wildtype TYK2 did not rescue IL-6 hyporesponsiveness in P1 cells, and TYK2 silencing in control or P1 cells did not alter IL-6 responses, indicating that P1's IL-6 defect was independent of the TYK2 mutation; they suggested it may underlie P1's staphylococcal disease and HIES features and that P1 may carry a variant in another unknown component of the IL-6 pathway.
quotes: Surprisingly, the responses of cells from P2, P3, P5, P7, and P8 were normal, at odds with the results for P1
These data indicate that the hyporesponsiveness to IL-6 of P1 did not result from a lack of TYK2.
The poor IL-6 responses seen in P1 but not in the other seven TYK2-deficient patients probably underlie at least the staphylococcal diseases, and perhaps other HIES phenotypes, of P1

findings.statement: Kreins et al. (2015) found normal numbers of central and effector memory CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in TYK2-deficient patients, unlike STAT3-mutated AD-HIES patients, suggesting viral reactivation results from impaired IFN-alpha/beta responses rather than a memory T-cell defect.
quotes: We observed that the TYK2-deficient patients P1, P2 (tested three times), P3, P4, and P5 had similar numbers of central memory (CD4+CCR7+CD45RA− and CD8+CCR7+CD45RA−) T cells to healthy controls

relevance_reason: Case report of a second TYK2-deficient patient, with clinical phenotype and homozygous TYK2 variant; shows the disorder can occur without HIES features.

findings.statement: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born to first-cousin parents, who developed disseminated BCG disease after vaccination at 2 months of age. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months, and generalized fistulous cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy with fever developed by 21 months. M. bovis BCG was isolated from discharging sinuses, and lymph node histology showed acid-fast bacilli. He recovered without relapse after 18 months of antimycobacterial therapy.
quotes: He was born in 1992 and was the third child of healthy, first-cousin parents. The patient was vaccinated with BCG at two months. At eight months, left axillary lymphadenopathy was detected
M. bovis BCG was isolated from the discharging cervical sinuses.
His clinical condition improved, with no relapse.

findings.statement: Kilic et al. (2012) reported that at age 8 years the patient developed neurobrucellosis, with seizures, neck stiffness and Brucella-positive blood and CSF cultures. It left him with severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with acyclovir and did not recur.
quotes: The blood and CSF cultures were positive for Brucella spp.
Neurobrucellosis caused severe neurological sequels including sensorineural hearing loss and cognitive impairment in our patient.
At 11 years, the patient was hospitalized with herpes zoster of the right maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve.

findings.statement: Unlike the first reported Japanese TYK2-deficient patient, the patient described by Kilic et al. (2012) had no features of hyper-IgE syndrome: no atopy, asthma, eczema, staphylococcal or candidal skin infections, and no skeletal or dental abnormalities. His serum IgE ranged from 80 to 218 IU/ml, normal or only slightly elevated. Serum IgG, IgM and IgA levels, lymphocyte subsets and the NBT test were normal. The authors suggested that TYK2 deficiency should be considered in patients with BCG disease or other intramacrophage infections, particularly with severe herpesvirus infections, even without HIES features.
quotes: Moreover, the patient’s medical history did not include signs of atopy, asthma or skin problems such as candidiasis, boils, folliculitis or cold abscess.
Serum IgE concentration were determined at the ages of 2, 11, 16 and 18 years, and were found to be normal or slightly high [80, 115, 218, 155 IU/ml, respectively]

a diagnosis of Tyk2 deficiency should be contemplated in patients with BCG clinical disease, particularly in the presence of unusually severe herpes virus infections, even in the absence of cardinal features of HIES.

findings.statement: Kilic et al. (2012) found that the Turkish patient was homozygous for a 9-bp deletion in exon 16 of the TYK2 gene (c.2302_2310del), which creates a premature termination codon at position 767. No full-length TYK2 protein was detectable by Western blot in the patient's EBV-B cells.
quotes: The patient is homozygous for a 9bp deletion in exon 16 of TYK2, c.2302_2310del or 2302del9, which creates a premature termination codon at position 767.
As a result, there is no full-length TYK2 protein detectable by western blotting in EBV-B cells.

findings.statement: Kilic et al. (2012) proposed that loss of TYK2 impairs IL-12 signaling and IFN-gamma production, causing susceptibility to BCG and Brucella. They suggested that the viral illnesses are probably related to an impaired cellular response to IFN-alpha/beta.
quotes: The absence of Tyk2 thus resulted in defective IL-12 signaling, leading to impaired IFN-γ production and susceptibility to BCG and Brucella.
These viral illnesses are probably related to an impaired cellular response to IFN-α/β, and are not seen in patients with AD HIES.

findings.statement: Woellner et al. (2007) addressed the relationship between the hyper-IgE syndrome and mutations in TYK2 in a correspondence.
quotes: The hyper IgE syndrome and mutations in TYK2.

relevance_reason: First report of human TYK2 deficiency: a homozygous TYK2 mutation in a patient diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome who had mycobacterial, viral and fungal infections. The paper also describes the cytokine signaling defects and their rescue.

findings.statement: Minegishi et al. (2006) described a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome. The patient was unusually susceptible to various microorganisms, including viruses, fungi, and mycobacteria, and had atopic dermatitis with elevated serum IgE.
quotes: a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome
This patient showed unusual susceptibility to various microorganisms including virus, fungi, and mycobacteria and suffered from atopic dermatitis with elevated serum IgE.

findings.statement: Minegishi et al. (2006) identified a homozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene in a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome. The abstract does not specify the mutation.
quotes: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome.

findings.statement: Minegishi et al. (2006) found that the patient's cells had defects in several cytokine signaling pathways, including those for type I interferon, IL6, IL10, IL12, and IL23. Transducing intact TYK2 restored these signals. The authors concluded that TYK2 deficiency likely accounted for the patient's complex clinical features, including impaired Th1 differentiation and accelerated Th2 differentiation.
quotes: The patient's cells displayed defects in multiple cytokine signaling pathways including those for type I interferon (IFN), interleukin (IL)-6, IL-10, IL-12, and IL-23.
The cytokine signals were successfully restored by transducing the intact Tyk2 gene.

Thus, the Tyk2 deficiency is likely to account for the patient's complex clinical manifestations, including the phenotype of impaired T helper 1 (Th1) differentiation and accelerated Th2 differentiation.

findings.statement: Minegishi et al. (2006) concluded that in humans TYK2 plays obligatory roles in multiple cytokine signals involved in innate and acquired immunity, and that this differs substantially from TYK2 function in mice.
quotes: demonstrates that Tyk2 plays obligatory roles in multiple cytokine signals involved in innate and acquired immunity of humans, which differs substantially from Tyk2 function in mice.
